meta.title: Who really said "To reach a port we must sail, sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it. But we must sail, and not drift, nor lie at anchor"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not FDR's wording: the line is Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.'s, from The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858). FDR quoted a shortened form in a 1938 fireside chat.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'To reach a port we must sail, sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it. But we must sail, and not drift, nor lie at anchor'?
meta.ogDescription: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. wrote it in The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858). FDR borrowed a shortened version to close his April 14, 1938 fireside chat.

answer.label: Not Franklin D. Roosevelt — actually Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
answer.sourceLine: The sentence comes from Holmes’s The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, chapter 4 (1858), where it reads “To reach the port of heaven, we must sail…”. The popular version changes that to “a port.” Roosevelt did borrow the image, but only a shortened form: he closed his fireside chat of April 14, 1938 with “For to reach a port, we must sail — sail, not lie at anchor, sail, not drift.”

source.heading: Where the words actually appear

docMeta.dd: 1858 (book); text shown from the 1873 James R. Osgood and Company edition

source.excerpt: I find the great thing in this world is not so much where we stand, as in what direction we are moving: To reach the port of heaven, we must sail sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it,—but we must sail, and not drift, nor lie at anchor.
trail: Holmes’s original sentence, with “the port of heaven,” is in chapter IV of The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table. The Project Gutenberg text ↗ was transcribed from the 1873 Osgood edition.

Wikiquote’s Holmes Sr. page ↗ lists the passage under Autocrat ch. 4. It adds that Josephus Daniels sent it to FDR on January 1, 1936, suggesting he use it “in one of your ‘fireside’ talks” (Kilpatrick, Roosevelt and Daniels, 1952, p. 159).
Roosevelt ended his fireside chat of April 14, 1938 (Miller Center transcript) ↗ with “For to reach a port, we must sail -- sail, not lie at anchor, sail, not drift.”

The same closing line appears in the Teaching American History text of the “Fireside Chat on the Recession” ↗. Neither transcript contains the “sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it” clause.
source.excerptNote: The version credited to Roosevelt is this sentence with “the port of heaven” changed to “a port” and its punctuation changed. What Roosevelt actually said on air, on April 14, 1938, was shorter: “For to reach a port, we must sail — sail, not lie at anchor, sail, not drift.”

author.name: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
author.heading: About Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.
author.bio: Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. was a Boston physician, professor and poet. He is best remembered for the essays he gathered as The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table (1858), table-talk spoken by a boarding-house “Autocrat.” He was the father of Supreme Court Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes Jr., and the two are often confused in quotation collections.

copyAttribution: "To reach the port of heaven, we must sail sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it,—but we must sail, and not drift, nor lie at anchor." — Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, ch. 4 (1858). Often credited to Franklin D. Roosevelt, who used a shortened version ("For to reach a port, we must sail — sail, not lie at anchor, sail, not drift.") in his fireside chat of April 14, 1938.

misattribution.heading: How a Holmes sentence became an FDR quote
misattribution.intro: Roosevelt is not a random target here. He really did use Holmes’s sailing image on the radio, and that true connection is how Holmes’s longer sentence came to circulate under FDR’s name.

items.why: He closed his April 14, 1938 fireside chat ↗ with “For to reach a port, we must sail -- sail, not lie at anchor, sail, not drift.” That is a compressed form of Holmes’s idea. It does not include the “sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it” sentence now quoted under his name.

According to Wikiquote ↗, citing Carroll Kilpatrick’s Roosevelt and Daniels (1952), Daniels, then ambassador to Mexico, mailed the Holmes passage to Roosevelt with his New Year greetings on January 1, 1936. He said it was “so good you may find a use for it in one of your ‘fireside’ talks.”

misattribution.truthLine: The full sentence belongs to Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr., The Autocrat of the Breakfast-Table, chapter IV (1858), where it reads “To reach the port of heaven…” (Project Gutenberg text ↗). Roosevelt spoke only a shortened version, in 1938.

context.heading: Why the line stuck to Roosevelt
lead: Roosevelt used the image at the very end of his April 14, 1938 fireside chat, which the Miller Center titles “On the Recession.” Just before it he said that abandoning his program “would be to miss the tide and perhaps to miss the port. I propose to sail ahead.” A nautical close suited a president known for his love of the sea, and the line has been repeated under his name ever since.

Later quote collections seem to have merged FDR’s spoken line with Holmes’s fuller sentence: they keep Roosevelt’s secular “a port” but restore Holmes’s “sometimes with the wind and sometimes against it.” That merger is our reading of the texts. No source we found documents exactly when or where it happened.
